title: Variance, Win Rates and Bankroll
intro: Even a strong player loses for weeks at a time, and a weak one can win for a month. This page measures how much luck there is in poker results: the standard deviation of a win rate, how many hands it takes to know whether you are a winner, how likely a bankroll is to go broke, and how big a bankroll should be.

items: Win rate in cash games is measured in big blinds won per 100 hands (bb/100). A good online six-handed regular might make 3 to 8 bb/100 after rake; a very strong one more. In limit games it is often given in big bets per 100 hands (BB/100).
Hourly rate is used live, where only about 25 to 35 hands are dealt an hour at a full table, against hundreds an hour for an online player using several tables.
In tournaments, return on investment (ROI) is profit divided by total buy-ins. Results are so lumpy that many hundreds or thousands of tournaments are needed to measure it.

Standard deviation (SD) measures how widely results swing, also per 100 hands. Typical figures are about 60 to 80 bb/100 for full-ring no-limit hold'em, 80 to 100 bb/100 for six-handed and well over 100 for heads-up or pot-limit Omaha. Aggressive styles have larger SD.

blocks.text: Hands are close to independent, so over many hands the total result is close to normally distributed (the central limit theorem). After $N$ hands, with win rate $w$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ (both per 100 hands), the expected result and its spread are:

blocks.caption: About 95% of results fall within 1.96 SD of the mean. The spread grows with the square root of the hands played, the mean grows in proportion to them.

blocks.text: So luck shrinks relative to skill only slowly. A player making 5 bb/100 with an SD of 90 bb/100 has, after 10,000 hands, an expected result of +500 bb but a 95% range of about +500 $\pm$ 1,764 bb: they lose money over those 10,000 hands about 29% of the time. After 100,000 hands the range is +5,000 $\pm$ 5,578 bb, and they are behind only about 4% of the time.
How many hands to know your win rate
Turn it round: after $N$ hands, the measured win rate has a 95% confidence interval of

blocks.caption: in bb/100. With $\sigma = 90$: $\pm 17.6$ after 10,000 hands, $\pm 5.6$ after 100,000, $\pm 1.8$ after a million.

blocks.text: To show at 95% confidence that a 5 bb/100 player is a winner at all takes about 125,000 hands, roughly what a part-time player plays in years and a full-time online professional in a few months. Short samples prove almost nothing, which is why reviewing decisions (by EV) teaches more than reviewing results. All-in adjusted results take out the luck of all-in hands and narrow the spread somewhat, but most variance comes from hands decided without an all-in.

Every winning player has long losing stretches. A downswing of 10 to 20 buy-ins (1,000 to 2,000 bb) over a few tens of thousands of hands is ordinary for a solid winner in a six-handed game, and break-even stretches of 50,000 hands or more happen. Knowing this protects against two mistakes: quitting a winning game because of a run of bad results, and tilting, playing worse because of them.

Risk of ruin (RoR) is the chance that a bankroll is lost entirely before it grows. Treating results as a random walk with drift, a player with win rate $w$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ (in the same units, per 100 hands) and a bankroll of $B$ big blinds who never moves down in stakes has

blocks.caption: For a losing or break-even player ($w \le 0$) the risk of ruin is 100%: a big enough bankroll only delays it.

blocks.text: The second curve shows the same player at half the win rate. Since a player never knows their true win rate exactly, and it falls as games get tougher, planning on the lower curve is wise. Two lessons stand out: risk falls exponentially with bankroll, so a few more buy-ins buy a lot of safety; and halving the win rate needs double the bankroll for the same risk.

items: Bankroll management is a rule for which stakes to play given the money set aside for poker. Common guidelines for players who rely on the bankroll: 20 to 50 buy-ins for cash games, 50 to 100 or more for sit-and-gos, and 100 to 300 or more for multi-table tournaments, whose variance is far larger.

Moving down in stakes after losses cuts the real risk of ruin far below the formula's, which assumes fixed stakes. Taking shots, playing a few sessions at a higher stake with a small slice of the bankroll, is how players move up.

The Kelly criterion, which maximises the long-run growth rate of a bankroll, argues the same way: when the edge is small relative to the variance, the amount risked at once should be a small fraction of the whole.
Recreational players who top up from income need less. The guidelines are for money that has to last.

blocks.title: Losing over a sample
blocks.text: A 5 bb/100 winner with an SD of 90 bb/100 plays 50,000 hands. What is the chance they finish behind?
blocks.hint: Find the mean and SD of the total over 500 blocks of 100 hands, then the normal probability of a result below zero.
solution: Zero is $2500/2012 \approx 1.24$ SD below the mean. A normal variable falls more than 1.24 SD below its mean about 10.7% of the time.

blocks.title: Bankroll for a target risk
blocks.text: A player's win rate is 5 bb/100 and their SD is 90 bb/100. What bankroll gives a 1% risk of ruin at fixed stakes?
solution: That is about 37 buy-ins of 100 bb. If the true win rate were 2.5 bb/100, it would take about 75.
